title: DNS and domains: could someone hijack your domains or your DNS?
short: Put phishing-resistant MFA on every registrar and DNS account this month, registry-lock the domains you sign in and mail with, and send all user DNS through a resolver you control.
answer: This month, put phishing-resistant MFA on every registrar and DNS provider account, registry-lock the few domains that sign-in, email and your website depend on, and publish CAA records on every domain. Then send all user DNS through a validating, filtering resolver you control, and sign zones with DNSSEC only where your provider automates the keys.
audience: IT and security teams in organizations of any size that own domains, run public DNS and resolve DNS for their users

blocks.title: If you only do five things

items.title: Put phishing-resistant MFA on every registrar and DNS account.
items.text: In the campaign behind CISA's ED 19-01, attackers used stolen credentials to change DNS records, then got valid certificates to decrypt the redirected traffic[^ed1901]. Use security keys or passkeys.

items.title: Registry-lock the domains everything depends on.
items.text: A registrar lock lasts only until someone in your registrar account asks for its removal. A registry lock is set by the registry and takes longer to remove[^eppcodes]; DENIC's .de lock needs a named contact to confirm each change[^denicrl]. Lock the domains behind sign-in, email, your website and name servers.

items.title: Make expiry impossible.
items.text: Use auto-renew on a company card, with more than one trusted person able to manage each domain[^ncscdomains]. Answer holder verification requests from your provider: unverified .de domains go offline[^denicverify].

items.title: Publish CAA everywhere and watch CT logs.
items.text: Name the CAs you use, publish `issue ";"` on domains that need no certificates[^rfc8659] and monitor certificate transparency logs for every domain, parked ones included[^googlecctld].

items.title: Send all user DNS through a resolver you control.
items.text: Validate DNSSEC, block known-bad domains with protective DNS, log queries and block DNS that goes around your resolvers[^sp80081].

blocks.title: If your domain or DNS is hijacked

items.title: Check the delegation at the registry.
items.text: Query the TLD's name servers for your NS and DS records. Your DNS provider's console can look normal while the domain points elsewhere.

items.title: Call your registrar and DNS provider.
items.text: Ask both to freeze the domain. If a gTLD domain was transferred away, only the registrars involved can file an ICANN transfer dispute, within 12 months[^tdrp], so push yours to act today.

items.title: Lock the attacker out and restore.
items.text: Change the passwords and MFA of every account that can change DNS records, and audit every public record on all authoritative servers, as ED 19-01 required[^ed1901]. Revoke API keys and compare against your last zone export.

items.title: Hunt down certificates.
items.text: Find certificates issued during the hijack in CT logs and report them to the issuing CA[^ed1901]. CAA can't stop issuance during a hijack, but CAA bound to your ACME account stops attackers reusing that validation afterwards[^googlecctld].

items.title: Treat redirected traffic as stolen.
items.text: Reset passwords of users who signed in during the window, rotate secrets sent by email and check the EU security laws sheet for reporting duties.

blocks.title: Registrar and DNS provider accounts
items: **One owner, several hands.** Move domains out of personal, agency and hosting accounts into ones your organization owns, and have one internal group register every domain[^ncscdomains].
**Scope who can change records.** In Azure DNS, grant DNS Zone Contributor per zone and ReadOnly-lock zones that rarely change. A CanNotDelete lock on the SOA record blocks deleting the zone[^azdns].
**Alert on NS and MX changes** and keep DNS change logs in your SIEM[^ncscdomains]. Export every zone weekly as a known-good copy.
**Report lookalikes to the registrar.** Monitor new registrations[^sp80081]. Registrars of gTLDs must act promptly on actionable evidence of phishing and other DNS abuse[^icannabuse].

blocks.title: DNSSEC and CAA
items: **Sign only where your provider automates the keys.** DNSSEC can't stop someone who logs in to your registrar or DNS provider, but it lets CAs detect forged CAA records[^rfc8659]. Use ECDSA P-256 or Ed25519; RSA/SHA-1 is deprecated[^icannalg].

**Know what breaks.** Since 15 March 2026, CAs must validate DNSSEC and can't issue on a validation error[^br], so a broken signature also blocks certificate renewals. Moving DNS provider? Remove the DS record first, as Route 53's migration steps do[^awsmigrate].

**Bind CAA to your ACME account.** Let's Encrypt honors `accounturi` now[^lecaa]. All CAs must from 15 March 2027, and email validation ends on 15 March 2028[^br]. Whoever controls your DNS will be able to get certificates.

blocks.title: What your resolvers should do
items: **Recurse only for your own clients.** No internet-facing server should be both authoritative and recursive[^sp80081].
**Validate DNSSEC** with automatic trust anchor updates, two time sources and QNAME minimization[^sp80081].
**Block DNS that goes around them:** outbound port 53 except from your resolvers, port 853 and known public DoH servers[^sp80081].
**Log queries.** Always log blocked queries, and keep a full log for forensics even if the SIEM gets less[^sp80081].

**Practice turning off validation for one zone.** In the .de outage of 5 May 2026, validating resolvers failed even for unsigned .de domains for about three hours; some large operators suspended validation for .de[^denicout].

blocks.title: Protective DNS and DNS over HTTPS
items: **Use a free service if it fits.** UK central government must use the NCSC's free PDNS[^ncscpdns]. DNS4EU runs a free public protective resolver with DoH and DoT, and offers DNS4GOV to public institutions[^dns4eu].
**Or buy one with logs and an API.** Ask for current deny lists, editable allow lists and block logs your SIEM can pull. It doesn't replace your own DNS logs[^ncscpriv].

**Control DoH in browsers.** Chrome sends no DoH on managed devices unless the `DnsOverHttpsMode` policy allows it[^chromedoh]. Firefox's DoH bypasses your DNS unless the `DNSOverHTTPS` policy's `ProviderURL` points at your resolver[^ffdoh].

blocks.title: What changed in 2026
items: **Three ccTLD registries were hijacked.** Attackers compromised the registries of .gh, .sl and .as, changed DNS records and got certificates for Google and other brands. Google advises restrictive CAA with ACME account bindings[^googlecctld].
**The root zone has a new key.** KSK-2024 (key tag 38696) has signed it since 11 October 2026. Check each validating resolver's trust anchors instead of assuming automatic updates worked[^ksk].

**.de verifies holder data.** Under NIS2, DENIC has risk-checked holder data since December 2025, now including a phone number, and existing domains must be verified too[^denicreg][^denicverify]. Real requests come through your provider, and DENIC never asks for passwords by email[^denicverify].

**Windows DNS Server speaks DoH.** Since the June 2026 update, Windows Server 2025 accepts DoH from clients, but not toward upstream servers[^kb5094125]. Clients can encrypt DNS without bypassing your resolver.

blocks.title: What you can skip
items: **Buying every typo and new TLD.** Register near-misses of sign-in and payment domains; monitor and report the rest.
**Signing internal zones.** NIST advises against it unless a rule requires it[^sp80081].
**NSEC3 to hide your zone.** It often still reveals every name; NIST calls NSEC the more prudent choice[^sp80081].

blocks.title: Mistakes that cost the most
items: **Domains in an account that can close.** Closing an AWS account suspends its Route 53 domains on day 5[^awsdomains]. Keep domains in an account nobody closes.
**Recovery email on the domain itself.** If the domain lapses, warnings can't reach you[^awsdomains]; if it's hijacked, the attacker gets your resets.
**Deleting the zone, not the delegation.** Anyone who opens an account at that DNS host can take over the name[^sp80081].

blocks.title: What this looks like at your size

columns.title: Small team, no security staff
items: Move every domain into a registrar account you own, with two admins on security keys.
Turn on auto-renew and registrar lock everywhere, and CAA for your one CA.
Point your router or firewall at a protective resolver such as DNS4EU's[^dns4eu].

columns.title: Growing, with IT or security staff
items: Registry-lock the critical domains, export zones weekly and alert on NS and MX changes.
Run validating resolvers with protective DNS and set browser DoH policies.
Rehearse the hijack steps yearly with your registrar's real contacts.

columns.title: Enterprise or regulated
items: Consolidate at one corporate registrar with registry lock and named contacts.
Require two-person approval for registrar and DNS changes.
If you provide DNS for others, check NIS2 scope in the EU security laws sheet.
